3.2 Process of Kalamkari Block Printing: a) Grey Cloth Cutting: Batches of 100 meters or above are purchased from textile mills in bulk.
The grey cloth purchased is then cut into pieces of length varying from 10 -15 meters as per the working unit capacity and customer demand/ end use.
b) Bleaching Cora Cloth: bleaching process is carried out using buffalo dung solution without using bleaching powder and facilitated by sunshine. It takes 4-5 days for getting the cloth white.
The kora long cloth which is cut to the required sizes is soaked in a goat or buffalo dung solution in a big pot.
The cloth is kept soaked throughout the night and the next morning it is
cleaned in the flowing water of a river or canal and then dried on the water weeds. This bleaching process is repeated for four or five days

No chemical bleaching powder should be uscd in this process. It is believed that the usage of bleaching powder will adversely affect the strength of the cloth as also will have a deleterious effect on the dyes applied

In order to make fibre more absorbent to obtain more even shades, penetration of the dye stuff the natural impurities have to be removed by boiling the cloth in hot alkaline solution like soda ash and caustic soda or detergent for 2-3 hrs at boiling temperature.

c) Application of Myrobalam: the white cloth is soaked in myrobalam juice in suach a way that it is equally distributed all over the cloth. It is then dried in sunlight. Myrobalam acts as a mordant for block printing.

d) Block Printing: It is the actual printing of designs/ motifs on the fabric by the use of wooden blocks and is done manually. The dyestuff/mordant of the desired color is applied to the fabric using blocks (outline, background and filling).

One block is needed for each colour of the motif to be printed on fabric.

The art of Block engraving involves cutting a design in relief upon blocks of wood, so that the raised parts, when charged with the colour, will transfer the design to the fabric on which such an engraved block is stamped.
Very fine chisels of different shapes and sizes are used to cut relief on the block.
Blocks are carved using the relief process, where the positive area, which has the design that will be transferred onto the cloth, rises above the sunken negative area.
Teak wood is preferred b ecause of the fine grains and strength.
For making the blocks, a cross section of teakwood is generally used.
For the temple wood carvings, the longitudinal section of the wood is used. But, for the blocks, the cross section of the wood is needed.
Traditionally, the wooden blocks were made from solid teak wood and the intricate design was chiselled on to the surface.
Today, the blocks are made from lighter wood and come with standard designs.

The word 'Kalamkari' evolved when the Golconda Sultans called the craftsmen as 'kalamkars'. The pen or brush was the 'kalam'.

Around the 11th century, when the Persians travelled to the port of Maesolia (Now Machilipatnam) to make money, they discovered that there was fabric available in India, which was hand printed using blocks.
